newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-Canada salmon talks off, may resume.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Canada salmon talks off, may resume.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday cancelled the next round of negotiations with Canada over salmon fishing after Canadian authorities, frustrated by the slow pace of talks, seized four American trawlers.

The State Department said in a statement negotiations over dwindling salmon stocks in the Pacific Northwest that had been scheduled to resume on Friday were postponed "until a more favourable climate for discussions can be achieved."
"The Canadian actions are regrettably poisoning the atmosphere," said a State Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Canada and the United States have skirmished for years over salmon catches and pressure for a deal is mounting before this year's salmon run begins in the next few weeks.

One week ago the Canadians angrily halted talks when U.S. negotiators said they were not authorised to offer a specific catch reduction at the session. Canada is concerned about overfishing by American boats as salmon head through Alaskan waters into Canadian waters to breed.

In a statement from Ottawa on Tuesday night, Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said Canada was acting within its rights under international law and he regretted the U.S. action, but he added that Canada was prepared to resume negotiations.
"We are ready to re-engage in negotiations. I will be contacting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright as soon as possible to discuss the situation," Axworthy said.

After the talks collapsed Canada began enforcing a regulation that required all U.S. fishing boats passing through its waters on their way to fishing grounds to report to Canadian authorities and stow their fishing gear.
The United States "is not closing the door on other actions" to respond to the Canadian seizure of the fishing boats, the State Department official said.

He said the U.S. Navy was concerned about a threat made last Friday by the British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, who said he might end a lease to a seabed in Nanoose Bay used by the Navy for torpedo testing.

The skippers of the first three boats appeared in court in Port Hardy, British Columbia, on Tuesday. They pleaded guilty, were fined $222 ($300 Canadian) each and regained custody of their boats, said Fisheries Department official Bud Graham.
A fourth boat from Washington State was stopped off the British Columbia coast and seized on Tuesday.
In Washington state, Gov. Gary Locke met with Clark Tuesday in Seattle and asked him to work toward releasing the seized vessels and preventing more seizures.
"I am fearful that escalating events can only sour the climate and only drive us apart," Locke said at a joint news conference with Clark.
But Clark instead renewed his call for stronger action from the Canadian government, including a resumption of transit fees on U.S. fishing vessels, last imposed in 1994.

"It's my view that given the State Department's reaction today, given the fact that the season is so close, that Canada has to increase the pressure, and British Columbia will do what we can to do so as well," Clark said.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien in Vancouver defended the Canadian enforcement efforts and said he had talked to President Bill Clinton about the dispute.
"We enforce the Canadian law, that's what we're doing at this moment with the boats ... The more pressure we can bring about, we do," Chretien said.

In another effort to pressure the United States, British Columbia last week announced it will cancel the lease on an underwater military range used by U.S. submarines to test torpedoes. Chretien said on Tuesday that the move "might be useful" in spurring the United States to compromise.
In Alaska late on Tuesday Gov. Tony Knowles said the talks should resume among all parties with a stake in the salmon harvest -- fishermen from Alaska, British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest.
Knowles said they should be "the ones to determine a way around what has become a gridlock for 12 years."

"We were making great success, and then the federal (Canadian) government, for political reasons of their own, put some non-negotiable issues on the table, caused the negotiations to break down and then followed it up with this real reckless gunboat diplomacy."
